title: GPU Provisioning: Immutable State & DR Playbook
author: Priya Shah
content:
Summary:

This playbook defines Redwood's standard for provisioning GPU capacity using immutable infrastructure patterns, safe Terraform state management, and an actionable disaster recovery (DR) procedure for corrupted or lost remote state. It targets delivery teams and oncall engineers who operate GPU pools across cloud accounts and regions.

Scope:

- Applies to all GPU node pools managed by Terraform in accounts that host production Redwood inference clusters.
- Covers Terraform backend configuration, state locking, snapshot/backup cadence, emergency restore steps, and CI/CD guardrails for promotion.
- Does NOT describe application-layer failover (see eng-sre runbooks) or model-serving runtime internals.

Goals:

1. Ensure Terraform state is single source of truth with robust locking and encrypted backups.
2. Make node pools immutable: changes must occur via image promotion or full replacement instead of in-place mutation.
3. Provide a clear, tested DR procedure that returns capacity within SLA (see SLOs below) after state corruption or accidental deletion.
4. Produce reproducible CI/CD promotion steps that prevent accidental state drift during capacity emergencies.

Definitions and Key Concepts:

- Immutable node pool: A pool where node replacement is performed by spinning up new instances from a gold image and cordoning/draining old instances, rather than mutating instance attributes in-place.
- Remote state snapshot: Periodic encrypted copy of Terraform state stored in a secondary S3 bucket and registered in our DR index (DynamoDB table).
- State locking: Prevents concurrent Terraform applies using DynamoDB-based locks (AWS) or equivalent.

Architecture Overview (high level):

- Terraform controllers run in our CI/CD runners (GitHub Actions runner fleet in aws-ci account).
- Remote state lives in an encrypted S3 bucket per account/region: s3://redwood-tfstate-<account>-<region>, with a DynamoDB lock table: redwood-tf-lock-<account>-<region>.
- A scheduled Lambda (tf-state-backup) copies the state file to the DR bucket (s3://redwood-dr-tfstate) every 6 hours and records a manifest in dr-index table. Backups are retained 90 days by default.
- GPU images are built by the GPU image pipeline (see eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build). Node replacement is orchestrated by the k8s node-pool-controller which reads tags/labels produced by Terraform.

SLOs and Operational Thresholds:

| Item | Target | Alerting threshold | 
|---|---:|---:|
| Warm GPU buffer (available spare capacity) | >= 15% of reserved pool | < 12% for 10m -> page oncall |
| Recovery time after state corruption to restore minimal capacity | <= 90 minutes | > 90 minutes -> incident declared |
| Remote-state backup cadence | 6 hours | missed run -> pager |

Ownership and Contacts:

- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity team (oncall alias: infra-gpu-oncall@redwood.internal).
- Terraform backend and DR automation: infra/iac team.
- CI/CD promotion guard: eng-dx (developer experience) for runner/credentials.
- Pager: eng-sre for cross-account networking breakages.

Terraform backend (recommended standard):

Use a per-account/region backend with server-side encryption and DynamoDB locking. Example backend stanza (Terraform v1.5+):

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "redwood-tfstate-${var.account_id}-${var.region}"
    key            = "env/${var.workspace}/gpu-node-pools.tfstate"
    region         = var.region
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "redwood-tf-lock-${var.account_id}-${var.region}"
  }
}
```

- Backend must be provisioned via a bootstrap job that runs with strong cross-account roles; do NOT hardcode credentials in runner configuration.
- All state files require server-side SSE-KMS with a dedicated key: alias/redwood/tfstate.

Immutable GPU node pool module (pattern):

- Module responsibilities: ASG/GKE node pool resource, image_id variable, lifecycle preventing in-place instance modification, lifecycle hooks for graceful cordon/drain.
- Promotion flow: build image -> upload AMI/GCP image -> set module var image_id in a PR -> CI runs plan -> gated manual apply by infra owner for production.

Example usage snippet (simplified):

```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source    = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v2.1.0"
  account_id = var.account_id
  region     = var.region
  name       = "inference-gpu-pool-${var.cluster}"
  image_id   = var.gpu_image_ami
  size       = var.desired_size
  min_size   = var.min_size
  max_size   = var.max_size
}
```

CI/CD Guardrails and Promotion Policy:

- All changes to GPU node pools must go through the gpu-node-pool module and tagged module releases. Direct edits to provider resources in service repos are disallowed.
- Pull requests that change image_id must include: image build id, image bake logs link, canary rollout plan (if production), and a workload readiness check list.
- Automatic apply to production is disabled. A manual approver from infra/iac must click the GitHub Actions approval step for prod applies.

Runbook: State corruption or accidental deletion of Terraform state

1) Detection:
   - Pager triggered by missing remote-state backup copy, unlock error alarms from DynamoDB, or failure of scheduled tf-state-backup.
2) Initial Triage (10 minutes):
   - Check S3 bucket for most recent object: aws s3 ls s3://redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region>/env/<workspace>/ --recursive --human-readable
   - Check DynamoDB lock table: aws dynamodb get-item --table-name redwood-tf-lock-<acct>-<region> --key '{"LockID": {"S": "tfstate-lock"}}'
   - If lock exists and owner is hung (older than 30 minutes), escalate to infra-iac to coordinate safe unlock.
3) Emergency restore path (if state is missing or corrupted):
   - Identify most recent healthy snapshot from dr-index: Query dr-index DynamoDB for key = tfstate-<acct>-<region>-env-<workspace> with latest timestamp.
   - Copy snapshot to the primary bucket: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-dr-tfstate/<snapshot-key> s3://redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region>/<state-key> --sse aws:kms --sse-kms-key-id alias/redwood/tfstate
   - Validate integrity: aws s3api head-object --bucket redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region> --key <state-key> and compare ETag against manifest.
   - Run a terraform state list against a read-only plan to confirm resources: terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform plan -refresh-only -var-file=secrets.tfvars
   - If plan shows unexpected drift for GPU pools, coordinate a controlled re-apply with infra-iac (see below).
4) Forcing an unlock (only if owner is unreachable and lock older than 60 minutes):
   - Document current lock item (export JSON).
   - aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name redwood-tf-lock-<acct>-<region> --key '{"LockID": {"S": "tfstate-lock"}}' --condition-expression 'attribute_exists(LockID) AND LockAge > :age' --expression-attribute-values '{":age": {"N": "3600"}}'
   - Note: Manual unlock must be recorded in incident ticket and commit message for the apply referencing the ticket ID.
5) Reconciliation:
   - If resources are missing at cloud level, prefer to re-create via Terraform apply rather than manual console fixes. Use a small controlled apply targeting only the GPU node-pool module: terraform apply -target=module.gpu_node_pool -auto-approve (only after peer review).
   - If the apply will recreate instances, coordinate maintenance window with product stakeholders if capacity impact > 10%.
6) Post-incident:
   - Create a postmortem within 72 hours documenting root cause, timeline, restore steps, and follow-ups.
   - Run a DR tabletop within 14 days if manual intervention was required.

Emergency GPU capacity expansion (if immediate compute is needed and Terraform restore will take too long):

- Short-lived escalation procedure (acceptable only for up to 4 hours):
  1. Use a pre-approved, audit-logged runbook user (role: rdb-emergency-provisioner) to launch additional instances from the latest gold image via cloud console/CLI.
  2. Tag instances with provenance: redwood:provision_method=emergency, redwood:incident_id=<INC1234>.
  3. Update k8s node labels/taints via kubectl to match expected selectors: kubectl label node <NODE> node.kubernetes.io/gpu-pool=inference && kubectl taint nodes <NODE> dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule-
  4. Notify infra-iac to persist these instances back into Terraform after state is restored by creating a terraform import plan.

Testing and DR Exercises:

- Schedule: Full DR restore test annually, partial restore (restore state and run readonly plan) every quarter.
- Test steps:
  - Start from last backup in DR bucket, restore to staging backend, run terraform plan, validate node-pool sizes, run a canary redeploy in staging, and measure time to recovery.
  - Capture metrics: time-to-restore, number-of-manual-steps, number-of-errors.

Change and Review Process:

- Any change to backend config, lock table naming, or backup cadence must be proposed as an ADR and approved by infra/iac and eng-sre.
- Code owners: terraform-modules repo requires at least two approvals from infra/iac maintainers before merge.

Appendix: Common commands and snippets

- Check remote state objects:
  aws s3 ls s3://redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region>/env/<workspace>/ --human-readable --summarize

- Force unlock (document and run only after approval):
  aws dynamodb delete-item --table-name redwood-tf-lock-<acct>-<region> --key '{"LockID": {"S": "tfstate-lock"}}'

- Restore snapshot from DR bucket:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-dr-tfstate/<snapshot-key> s3://redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region>/<state-key> --sse aws:kms --sse-kms-key-id alias/redwood/tfstate

- Validate plan against restored state (read-only):
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-tfstate-<acct>-<region>" -backend-config="key=env/<workspace>/gpu-node-pools.tfstate"
  terraform plan -refresh-only -var-file=secrets.tfvars

Maintenance and housekeeping:

- Backup retention: 90 days for DR snapshots; move older artifacts to cold storage (glacier) after 90 days if required by compliance.
- Rotate KMS keys for tfstate every 365 days; coordinate with infra security.
- Monthly audit: infra-iac runs a job that verifies every account/region has a backend bucket, a lock table, and a DR snapshot from the last 24 hours. Failures create a ticket in the infra backlog.
